audience.description: Undergraduate calculus, basic probability and linear algebra; expected value, variance, standard deviation and density are known. Earlier Part I teaches Brownian increments, local diffusion, stochastic conventions and neutral projection. These subject-specific prerequisites were read in actual source and are not treated as audience assumptions.

relations.evidence: Actual earlier mechanism distinguishes fixed mismatch producing repeatable bias from changing noise producing different trial trajectories. This supports separating mean error from spread without a new elementary-statistics lesson.
The opening requires the reader to distinguish repeatable pull, wandering state and poor readout; the earlier fixed-versus-changing mechanism supplies that distinction.
Mean error and variance are reported separately because cue-specific bias and trial spread answer different questions.
Defines systematic angular motion b and half the local variance growth rate D, then relates them to conditional increment means and variances with local assumptions.
The example compares variance alone with variance plus squared mean error; the reader must keep bias separate from random spread.
Explains how attraction to preferred states reduces random spread while biasing other cues, gives the pinning definition, and states why both mean and variance matter.
Testing between preferred positions detects attraction to discrete preferred states, rather than testing only cues already at those states.
The lower-variance circuit has worse MSE because attraction creates a nonzero mean error. This is the taught pinning mechanism with checked arithmetic.
The definition says to add or subtract complete turns at 0/360 crossings to continue the trajectory. This states the operation before its sampling condition is used.
The following instruction restricts use to sampling that can identify crossings, acknowledging that sparse observations can hide turns.
The long-delay instruction uses the distinction between continued trajectories and angular error modulo a full turn. It explicitly states why full-turn-separated values are the same angle.

The passage identifies local activity dynamics, Brownian noise map, left neutral vector and coordinate normalization. The displayed equation immediately following this indexed paragraph was read directly: D=ell^T B B^T ell/2. The earlier Part I derivation linked at its start supplies stable transverse modes and the left/right distinction. This is adequate combined teaching, not an inference from a label or link alone.
Corrected versus surviving disturbance directions explain why total noise magnitude alone does not fix decoded diffusion.
The derivation uses the normalized left vector to remove linear deterministic drift and compute coordinate-noise covariance.

Defines model and physical time with t_m=a t_p, substitutes the mapping in variance growth, and obtains D_p=a D_m per physical second. The reader can follow the substitution with the declared algebra background.
The following sentences interpret this mapping as ideal rescaling and explain why communication, temperature and readout can break it in a real device.
